title: A Giant Hug on the Grass: 23,000 Square Feet of Art Brings a City Together
summary:
Imagine lying on your back in a park and seeing two giant arms reaching across the grass, their hands clasped in a friendly grip. That's what you'd see if you visited Boom Island Park in Minneapolis this month! A French-Swiss artist named Saype painted a massive picture right onto the lawn. It's 310 feet long and 75 feet wide—that's longer than a basketball court and wider than a tennis court!

The painting shows two arms coming together in a handshake or a hug. It's part of Saype's "Beyond Walls" project, where he travels the world creating art that connects people. He uses a special paint that's completely biodegradable, which means it's safe for the grass and will slowly fade away with rain and mowing. No harm to nature!

Minneapolis has been through some tough times, but the people there are known for helping each other out—like shoveling a neighbor's sidewalk after a snowstorm. Saype said he found "incredible humanity" in the city. On the first weekend of June, hundreds of residents came to watch him work. Then they did something amazing: they formed a human chain around the painting, linking arms to show they stand together. It was a powerful reminder that art can make us feel connected, even when we're far apart. You can even buy a print of the artwork to help Saype create more giant hugs around the world!
why_it_matters: Just like a hug can make you feel better, this giant grass hug reminds us that when communities support each other — even with small acts like shoveling a walkway — the whole city becomes stronger.

background_read: Land art is a type of art drawn directly onto fields, snow, or beaches; the giant chalk figures carved into hillsides in England are famous examples.
Saype (a French-Swiss artist born in 1989) is known for huge, biodegradable paintings on grass in places like the Swiss Alps, Paris, and now Minneapolis.
Minneapolis (a city in Minnesota) is known for its cold winters, where neighbors often help each other shovel sidewalks, so the human chain reflects that community spirit.

perspectives.description: They see the painting as a beautiful, temporary gift that brings people together in a shared moment of wonder, and they love that it doesn't hurt nature.
Some might wonder if a painting that fades quickly is worth the effort, or if the money could have been spent on other community needs.
They see the project as a thoughtful way to use public space for art, and they note that even a short-lived artwork can leave a lasting feeling of connection.
